notes.b: The skeleton has two parts, and the axial skeleton is the one that forms the central axis (the upright line) of the body. The appendicular skeleton, the limbs and the girdles that attach them, is attached to it. There is more on this in The appendicular skeleton.
points: The axial skeleton is made of four parts: the skull, the vertebral column (the vertebrae, which are the individual back bones, plus the discs between them), the ribs and the sternum (breastbone).
Its main jobs are protecting the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs, which are soft and easily damaged, and supporting the head and trunk (the body without the head and limbs).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name the parts of the axial skeleton. Learn the four: skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum. The pelvic girdle, clavicle and scapula belong to the appendicular skeleton, not this one.

notes.b: The skull is the bony case of the head. It protects the brain and the sense organs, and it is built from two parts with different jobs.
points: The skull has two parts. The cranium is a dome of curved, flat bones that encloses and protects the brain.
The facial bones form the face, hold the teeth, and form the eye sockets (orbits) and the nasal cavity (the space inside the nose).

The bones of the cranium are joined by sutures: wavy, interlocking joints filled with fibrous tissue that allow no movement, so the cranium acts as one rigid, strong box. Its domed shape also spreads the force of a blow.
The lower jaw (mandible) is the only skull bone that moves. It joins the cranium at a freely movable joint on each side, allowing chewing and speech.
The skull also protects the sense organs: the eyes sit in the bony orbits, and the inner ear is enclosed in bone.
A large opening at the base of the cranium, the foramen magnum, lets the spinal cord pass down from the brain. The skull rests on the first vertebra.

In a newborn baby the cranial bones are not yet fused (joined into one). Soft, membrane-covered gaps called fontanelles allow the skull to change shape slightly during birth and allow the brain to grow; they close in the first two years.
Diagram: side view of the skull, labelling cranium, sutures, orbit (eye socket), facial bones, upper jaw, lower jaw (mandible), teeth and foramen magnum (or opening for spinal cord).
notes.tip: Remember that the mandible is the only movable bone of the skull, and that the cranial sutures allow no movement. Examiners ask for the function of the skull, and a labelled diagram of it.

notes.h: The vertebral column and its regions
notes.b: The vertebral column is the backbone. It is made of many small bones stacked in a line, so it is strong enough to carry the body yet flexible enough to bend. It is divided into five regions, each suited to its job.
points: The vertebral column (backbone or spine) is a flexible column of 33 vertebrae stacked one on another, from the skull to the pelvis.
It supports the head and trunk, protects the spinal cord, provides attachment for ribs and muscles, and joins the axial skeleton to the pelvic girdle (the hip bones).
The 7 cervical vertebrae (neck) are small and light, so they can support the head and allow it to nod and turn.
The 12 thoracic vertebrae (chest) each join a pair of ribs.
The 5 lumbar vertebrae (lower back) are the largest and strongest. They carry most of the weight of the upper body and allow bending.
The 5 sacral vertebrae are fused into one bone, the sacrum, which is joined to the pelvic girdle and passes the body's weight to the legs.
About 4 coccygeal vertebrae are fused to form the coccyx (tailbone), which anchors some muscles; the number varies from 3 to 5.
Vertebrae get larger from the neck to the lower back, because each one carries the weight of everything above it.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name the regions of the column and to relate the size of the vertebrae to their position. Give the reason: the lower the vertebra, the more weight it carries.

notes.h: Atlas, axis and the curves of the spine
notes.b: The top two vertebrae are shaped differently from the rest so that the head can move in two ways. Seen from the side, the whole column also bends in an S shape.
points: The atlas (first cervical vertebra) carries the skull and allows the head to nod.
The axis (second cervical vertebra) has a peg on which the atlas turns, allowing the head to rotate from side to side.
The column has an S-shaped curve when seen from the side: forward in the neck, back in the chest and forward in the lower back.
The curves act like a spring, absorbing shock when walking and running, and keep the body's weight balanced over the legs.
Diagram: side view of the vertebral column labelling the cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and coccyx regions, the S-shaped curves and the discs between vertebrae.
notes.tip: Keep the two top vertebrae apart: the atlas is for nodding, the axis is for rotating, because the atlas turns on the axis's peg.

notes.b: A typical vertebra has a heavy part at the front to take weight, and a ring of bone at the back to protect the spinal cord. Each part of its structure suits its job.
points: The centrum (body) is a thick cylinder of bone at the front of the vertebra. It bears the body's weight.
The neural arch at the back surrounds the neural canal (vertebral canal), through which the spinal cord runs, so the cord is enclosed in bone.

The spinous process at the back and a transverse process on each side are projections that provide attachment for muscles and ligaments (tough bands that join bone to bone), acting as levers for the back muscles.
Facets are smooth surfaces that form small joints with the vertebrae above and below, guiding and limiting movement. In thoracic vertebrae, extra facets form the joints with the ribs.
Between neighbouring vertebrae there are small gaps on each side through which the spinal nerves leave the spinal cord. There is more on this in CNS and PNS.
Diagram: top view of a single lumbar or thoracic vertebra labelling centrum, neural arch, neural canal with spinal cord, spinous process, transverse processes and facets.
notes.tip: The neural canal with the spinal cord is at the back of the vertebra, behind the centrum, and the centrum is the part that bears weight. Examiners ask you to label a vertebra, so do not mix these up.

notes.b: Bone on bone would be painful and would wear away, and it would not bend. Between the vertebrae lie intervertebral discs (inter means between), which solve these problems.
points: Position: an intervertebral disc lies between the centra of each pair of neighbouring vertebrae, from below the axis down to the sacrum, joining them together.
There are no discs within the fused sacrum and coccyx, because those vertebrae are fused into single bones and do not move against each other.
Structure: each disc is a pad of cartilage with a tough outer ring of fibrocartilage (fibrous cartilage) surrounding a soft, jelly-like centre.
Shock absorption: the discs compress under load and spring back, cushioning the vertebrae and the brain against the jolts of walking, running and jumping.
Preventing friction and wear: the discs stop the bones of neighbouring vertebrae rubbing against each other.

Flexibility: each disc allows a small amount of movement between two vertebrae, so the joints between vertebrae are slightly movable. Added together along the column, these small movements let the back bend forwards, backwards and sideways, and twist.
Holding the column together: the discs, with the ligaments, bind the vertebrae into one column while allowing it to bend.
The discs are squeezed slightly during a day of standing and sitting and recover while lying down, so a person is slightly taller in the morning than in the evening.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the position and the functions of the discs. Say they lie between the centra (bodies) of the vertebrae, not between the spinous processes, and that they are cartilage, not bone or fluid sacs. Then give the functions: shock absorption, preventing friction, flexibility and holding the column together.

notes.b: The ribs and sternum together form the rib cage, a bony cage around the chest. It must be strong enough to protect the organs inside but also able to move, because the chest changes size when we breathe.
points: There are 12 pairs of ribs: curved, flat bones that form the rib cage around the chest. At the back, every rib is joined to a thoracic vertebra by small joints that let it move.
The first seven pairs (true ribs) are joined directly to the sternum by strips of flexible costal cartilage.
Pairs 8 to 10 (false ribs) are joined to the cartilage of the rib above them.
Pairs 11 and 12 (floating ribs) are attached only at the back, to the vertebrae, and are free at the front.
The rib cage protects the heart and lungs, and partly the liver, stomach and kidneys.

Because the ribs are curved and joined by flexible cartilage, the cage can absorb blows and can move. The intercostal muscles between the ribs raise and lower the rib cage, changing the volume of the chest in breathing. There is more on this in Gas exchange and the breathing mechanism.

The sternum (breastbone) is a long, flat bone in the centre of the front of the chest. It protects the heart and anchors the ribs, through the costal cartilages, and the clavicles (collarbones). Like other flat bones, it contains red bone marrow.
Diagram: front view of the rib cage labelling the sternum, ribs, costal cartilage, true, false and floating ribs, thoracic vertebrae (behind), and the position of the clavicles.
notes.tip: Floating ribs are still attached to vertebrae at the back; they are floating only at the front. For how the rib cage suits protection and breathing, give both reasons: curved and cartilage-joined ribs absorb blows, and the cage can move for breathing.

keyTerms.definition: The dome of curved, flat bones of the skull that encloses and protects the brain.
A wavy, immovable joint between the bones of the cranium, filled with fibrous tissue.
The large opening at the base of the cranium through which the spinal cord passes.
A soft, membrane-covered gap between the cranial bones of a newborn, which closes in the first two years.
The thick cylinder of bone at the front of a vertebra, which bears the body's weight.
The bony arch at the back of a vertebra that surrounds the neural canal and spinal cord.
A pad of cartilage between the centra of neighbouring vertebrae, which absorbs shock and allows slight movement.
Flexible cartilage that joins the ribs to the sternum and to each other.

questions.prompt: Where are the intervertebral discs found, and give two of their functions.
questions.model: The intervertebral discs lie between the centra of each pair of neighbouring vertebrae, from below the axis down to the sacrum. Two functions: they absorb shock, compressing under load and springing back to cushion the vertebrae and brain against the jolts of walking, running and jumping; and they allow a small amount of movement between vertebrae, so the back can bend and twist.

questions.prompt: Relate the structure of a vertebra to its functions. Include a labelled diagram.
questions.model: The centrum is a thick cylinder of bone at the front that bears the body's weight. The neural arch surrounds the neural canal, through which the spinal cord runs, so the cord is protected by bone. The spinous process and transverse processes project from the vertebra and provide attachment for muscles and ligaments, acting as levers for the back muscles. The facets are smooth surfaces that form small joints with the vertebrae above and below, guiding and limiting movement. A labelled diagram should show the centrum, neural arch, neural canal with spinal cord, spinous process, transverse processes and facets, with a top view of a lumbar or thoracic vertebra.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of (i) the cranium and (ii) the rib cage suits each to its function.
questions.model: (i) The cranium is a dome of curved, flat bones joined by sutures, which are wavy, interlocking joints that allow no movement. It forms one rigid, strong box that protects the brain, and its domed shape spreads the force of a blow. (ii) The rib cage is made of curved ribs joined at the back to thoracic vertebrae and at the front to the sternum by flexible costal cartilage. It protects the heart and lungs, and because the ribs can move, the intercostal muscles raise and lower the rib cage to change the volume of the chest in breathing.
